utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: With the Chamber's permission, I would like to inform it that at some point, and perhaps the earlier the better, we would like to ask for a very brief closed session to establish a matter that may affect the witness's sense of security. If the Court would like to do this now, I am certainly prepared to address it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do it now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to present to you some documents which were only gathered by the Office of the Prosecutor very quickly in response to your evidence, and therefore I apologise to the Chamber that we have only the Croatian or the Bosnian Serbian Croatian edition. If in fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not going to admit that. It's against the Rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I simply ask questions from the documents and see if the witness can identify them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'd appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can put something to him, but you can't put the documents in.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That's fine. I will have to ask that a copy of it be distributed to the witness and put on the ELMO, simply so that it can be seen. It will be Z350.1, which we will not ask for admission at this time; Z59.1 -- I'm sorry. 259.1. Those two at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Commander Totic, looking at -- sorry, Brigadier Totic, looking at 350.1 -- if it is visible to the interpreters; if not, I would ask that a copy be given -- they have one. This is a document signed by you on the 4th of January, 1993. Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you be kind enough to read it out? It is very brief. In that way, we will avoid having to attempt to get a written translation later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "This is a record on the turnover of materiels, of the technical materiel, between Zenica and Trosic, according to the leading document, which is in Zenica, with the HVO in Zenica."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. You're reading -- I had asked for 350.1. Did I -- unless I'm confused, I believe it was 350.1, the other document under your signature. I think we'd asked for that first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "This is a receipt confirming that Mr. Danimir Bilic was mobilised into the Croat Defence Council in Zenica on the 1st of April, 1992. He was at the front in Jajce on the 14th of October, 1992, and at Turbe between the 19th, 22nd December, 1992. He remains a member of the HVO in Jure Francetic Brigade. This certificate is issued for the regulation of his rights in the Republic of Croatia and for the issue of passport and other personal identification documents." I see nothing unusual there. The young man wanted to change to the Croatian army. He wanted to have his domovnica and his passport, and I did it because it's his right to live wherever he wants to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next document, Z259.1, it is -- without reading the whole document, it is a list, as you indicated, and the last paragraph, would you please read it into the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "All possible misunderstandings relative to these goods and materiel were resolved between the president of HVO Zenica Mr. Dominik Sakic and Mr. Vlado Knezevic, representative of the HV from Beograd." Your Honours, Tomislav Trosic, referred to here, was a member of the Foreign Legion, who arrived in Zenica owing to some of his relations, that is, Dominik Sakic, who was the HVO president. He brought certain things there, and he asked me to sign so that he could justify his trip when he went back to Croatia. And I said I could not do it, that I would keep this document, because he wanted to sell it, sell these things. So I sent him to the president of the HVO, Mr. Sakic, and Mr. Vlado Knezevic, because he said to him to bring this equipment there and he was a member of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier Totic, your relationship, your attitude toward political leaders, how would you characterise it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am a soldier, and at no time did I doubt the political leadership. I had no ambitions, nor do I have any, to engage in political life. I respected the political leadership.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier Totic, are you familiar with a magazine called Bojovnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Explain what Bojovnik is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, Bojovnik means a soldier. It is a Croat word for soldier, for a combatant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there a magazine that bears that name that is an HVO publication principally out of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is a magazine issued by the HVO Zenica, and its title was Bojovnik bass.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask the usher to distribute Z376.3. The English translation, to which I will be referring, appears on the second page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier Totic, there is a Croatian copy attached to this document. You were asked by the interviewer from Bojovnik magazine from January of 1993, which appeared in January of 1993, question: "Are you satisfied with the disposition and the area designated to the provinces ..." This is presumably about Vance-Owen, Mr. Totic. Your answer: "I am a soldier and I shall give my unreserved support to anything created or agreed upon by the elected Croat leaders. That is my duty, and I'm sure all the Croat soldiers shall do the same." Is that how you felt then and is this how you feel now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To this day, I feel and think that it is the soldier's duty to accept everything agreed upon by the lawful political leadership.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Z331 is also a Bojovnik article, and there's just a brief passage to which I shall be referring and ask you about. So you know, Brigadier, there has been film footage of the event of the swearing-in ceremony in Zenica, and the particular passage I would like to ask you about, and your reaction to it, is contained on the first page of the translation. It reads. It is by Dario Kordic, and Kordic is saying: "I am particularly pleased that we have turned out here today in such large numbers. I am pleased that we are here on Croatian territory, on the integral territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. The Croatian territory of Zenica was Croatian, it still is now, and will be Croatian territory. Therefore, it is now, and will be, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, whether some like it or not." Did you share that view that was expressed at the swearing-in ceremony? Is that your view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, as I saw it then, and today, is a community which was formed to protect Croat national interests throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. No division was ever raised as an issue, nor did I ever think about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One question. There is a reference on the cover page of the translation, the front page, which indicates that General Slobodan Praljak was also in attendance. Did you see General Praljak at that ceremony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I greeted him, General Praljak. Before that he [Realtime transcript read in error "I"] was an officer in the Croatian army. At the beginning of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, he returned to Bosnia-Herzegovina to defend his homestead, like many other Croats. General Praljak was born in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might just interrupt. There appears to be an error in the transcript. I'm sure it will be corrected, but it says, at page 33, line 23 to 24 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. There appears to be an error in the transcript. It says -- the English says, "Before that I was an officer in the Croatian army," and I think what Brigadier Totic was before that he was an officer in the Croatian army; i.e., General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Z444.1, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier Totic, this is an order of 6 February, 1993, signed by you, and I am interested only in paragraph 4 of the order. It is addressed, of course, to all members of your brigade, the Jure Francetic Brigade. It says: "In an appropriate manner, point out to all HVO members the enormous damage we do ourselves by the use of fascist greetings and all other greetings evocative of fascism. Zenica studio of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna may be used in the carrying out of this assignment." What prompted your issuing this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was prompted to issue this order by a simple reason, because at that time, in 1992, and even in 1993, there were individuals who wore also some insignia which could be associated with the fascists, with the Nazi party, and so forth. And the official view, the official position, was to fight against it, because we have nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The use of HV army insignia was a problem in your area, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it wasn't only the Croatian army insignia that were worn. I think there were more German insignia, because the uniforms that we -- the uniforms that we bought, I mean the state that we imported those uniforms from, simply had these insignia, and at the same time it was something of a fad at the time, something of a fashion at the time, to put on all sorts of insignia, different emblems.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would like to ask that Z293.1 be presented. In an unusual turn of interpreting fate, we have only a French translation, and we should hopefully have an English one for the Court, on this point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at paragraph 3 of an order that is signed by -- if you can tell the Court who Zoran Covic is, please. Who is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, Zoran Covic was my deputy. Before that, in early 1992, in early April, or rather early May, when the HVO was founded, he was the commander of the Croat staff for military matters. For a short while he was the commander of the Municipal Staff. And on the 29th of July, 1992, I took over from him the command of the staff in Zenica and he was my deputy. And later on he also was my deputy in Jure Francetic Brigade, I believe sometime in February 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to read out loud the very brief paragraph 3, and then it can be translated for the English-speaking Judges as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Members of the HV present in these lands with HV insignia should be warned to remove those insignia because in this manner we're merely involving, embroiling, the HV in these problems." That is Zoran Covic. And, Your Honours, I have already said there were no organised HV units, that it was individuals who came from the Republic of Croatia to defend Bosnia-Herzegovina, and with them they also brought their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the interrelations or the interaction between your brigade and the brigade in Busovaca, the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the relationship between me and the commander of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade were very fair. I often met the commander at meetings at the command of the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there, if you recollect, a fair amount of exchange of troops and materiel from your units down to Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we had to help one another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in order to achieve a state of full military readiness, or full combat readiness, did you also assist each other in arming and informing your troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me rephrase it. In order to obtain a state of full combat readiness, did you need to also help each other out, the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade receiving assistance from the Jure Francetic Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Assistance to one brigade or the other, anything that would be ordered from above through the chain of command would be done; that is, whatever was ordered by the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come back to this point. I need to locate some documents which have slipped to the bottom. In the meantime, I want to ask you about your evidence that if you had been given an order by Dario Kordic, your response, I believe, was that you would return the order up to the other chain of command, or the military chain of command. You testified that you were not aware of any order given by Kordic that had been, in fact, obeyed or carried out by any HVO member; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I do not know of any such order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This Chamber has seen, in the course of a number of witnesses, the testimony of a number of witnesses, Z100, which is an order issued by Dario Kordic on the 10th of May, 1992, ordering the arrest of Dzemal Merdan. You were aware, are you not, that Merdan was arrested? That is your testimony; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware, Your Honours, from the conversation Mr. Dzemal Merdan and myself, and he said that he had been arrested. I don't know anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it your answer is you did not know that Dario Kordic issued the order for this arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that, I do not know it, and I don't believe it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I ask you if you were aware of whether or not you know if Dario Kordic ordered the disbanding of the Territorial Defence in Busovaca in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask -- would the Court consider five minutes early, and then I would be able to try to consolidate some of these documents and get on with this a little bit quicker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we will, but how long -- how much longer do you anticipate being, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I will not go beyond the lunch break, that is for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now, half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Exhibit 371.2, Z371.2, please, which we will seek to introduce. And there is another one that we will not seek to introduce but rather only show the witness, for failure to have a translation, which is Z253.1. I will deal with them individually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, you have before you two documents, the first of which I would just ask you to look at. It is not translated, and therefore I will simply give you a bit of data and ask you to fill it in. It is a document under your signature, Z253.1, dated 24 October 1992, and the second point there indicates that: "All the forces of the HVO Zenica are in a state of full combat readiness." Can you tell the Judges, please, what was occurring at that time, and explain why you had your forces in full combat readiness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is only now that I see this document. Quite a bit of time has elapsed. I don't know exactly what was happening at the time. I just know that I issued this order on the basis of the order that I received from the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at the second document dated 16 January 1993, which we will seek to have admitted, Z371.2, the date of it is, as I said, 16 January 1993. Can you explain, please, why, under your signature, this order also puts your troops in a state of full combat readiness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the preamble it says: "On the basis of order number", et cetera, et cetera, "the Main Staff of the HVO," et cetera, so I only carried out orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have no independent recollection of why you put a large number of people in a state of full combat readiness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Briefly, you had indicated earlier, when we were discussing the relationship between your brigade and the Zrinjski Brigade in Busovaca, that there was, if you will, a philosophy to help one another. Can you recall roughly the number of times, under your order, assistance was rendered to that brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I cannot say exactly now how many times. I just know that I did give help.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Again, I'm not seeking to introduce these particular items, but I'm asking the usher merely to present them to the witness. They are under his hand. Please, if they could be put on the ELMO, it would be helpful to all of us. That is my copy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first document is dated, I believe, 15 February. Is that correct? It's a little difficult for me to see. 15 February 1993. What was the relationship in that document between your unit and the brigade in Busovaca, as expressed in paragraph 4? Just tell the Judges, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the unit is rallied together, it is put under the command of the brigade of Nikola Subic-Zrinjski in Busovaca. Your Honours, this happened after the incidents in Dusina. The Croatian population of the municipalities of Zenica and Busovaca have family ties. After that, I was put in a difficult position, in a moral dilemma, what to do. People went there consciously to defend it because Busovaca had been attacked. The unit that is mentioned here that is to be sent to Busovaca was established from the point of view of a formation, and it was immediately put under the command of Nikola Subic-Zrinjski. Their tasks were exclusively defensive, that is to say, the defence of Croatian villages, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that stated in the order, that it is exclusively defensive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew what this was about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please answer my question. Is that stated in the written order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not stated in the written order here, but I know what it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The next document, please. And any order is fine, since you have my copy. Can you please read the date of the document? And if you can lower it a bit, Mr. Usher, it would be helpful. Thank you. Sorry, that doesn't help. It's too fuzzy for us. Can you determine that, Brigadier, what the date of that document is that you signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Point 1, the 9th of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at point 4 of that document, what are you ordering?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The unit is placed under the command of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade in Busovaca. That is to say, when one shift returns, the other one is supposed to go. I do not have the right to command -- to issue orders in the zone of responsibility of other brigades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there anything on that document about the nature of the action or the nature of the assignment there, defensive or offensive; is it specified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next document, please. That one appears to be -- I'm sorry, Brigadier. Can you assist me in giving the date of that? Is it February? Is that a "2" in the middle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't see it very well. Possibly February.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what are you ordering in that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in this document I am ordering that the commander of the Mixed Anti-Armour Unit send five grenades for a plain recoilless gun to the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade. This shows quite clearly that we did not attack anyone, nor were we preparing to attack anyone. I said on Friday that we were logistically quite unprepared for the attack of the Muslim units on us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the word "attack" appear anywhere on that order? I must have missed it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The words are the following: "On the basis of expressed needs and in order to fill the ranks of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade." Your Honours, five grenades, if a brigade does not have five grenades, which commander would dare attack anyone? That is proof of the logistics position that we were in then. We did not even contemplate attacking someone. It was only defence that was our objective.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did I also miss "defence"? Is that word there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is not a combat order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'd like to ask the usher to present Z371.1. Again, those documents will not be -- the ones that have just been looked at will not be introduced. And also, just to look at and not to introduce, Z309.1. Two quick points on these orders. Looking at 371.1, just a quick question: Can you explain, please, in paragraph 1, where it says, "Personal weapons distributed from the HDZ, Croatian Democratic Union, and HVO" why -- where would the weapons for the HDZ have been used? Can you explain why the HDZ is holding weapons, please? That is a political party, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this order is dated the 16th of January, 1993. I ordered the exemption of personal weapons that were distributed from HDZ sources. You know that the people were self-organised and that arms were given to persons through the Crisis Staff of the HDZ. When it was established that these weapons were distributed to persons who were either not able-bodied or too old, I ordered that these weapons be exempted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, the HDZ is listed as a holder of weapons on the untranslated document, Z309.1, in paragraph 3. Is that also your explanation for why the HDZ, a political organisation, is holding weapons? If you look at paragraph 3, please, in the Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the HDZ did not possess weapons. Individuals who did have weapons and did not want to hand them over claimed that weapons were given to them by the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were appointed by Dominik Sakic to your position; is that correct? You were actually given the position of brigade commander by Sakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Dominik Sakic, as president of the HVO of Zenica, could only make a proposal. I was appointed through the order of the commander of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, and later of the commander of HZ HB, Mr. Mate Boban. That is the same way I was appointed brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then Sakic nominated you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibly he made this proposal, but I don't know of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I just ask you if this brings -- refreshes your recollection. It would be Z172.1. It is not to go into evidence. Just read it, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Could it be put on the ELMO, please, as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does it say about you in that particular decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says that he appointed me, but he did not appoint me. This is the first time I see this decision. He did not appoint me to this position. I personally never saw this decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This decision of 28 July 1992, from the HVO. Okay. Do you recall any instances where there was interaction between you and Sakic on matters of nomination or -- of nomination for various positions or of any political military decisions? Did you keep a separate role or were you closely allied in your work habits?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never had a political role, or was I ever interested in something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd just like to ask you if you could take a quick look at this document, which is Z244.1?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And also, Mr. Usher, if it's not difficult, Z451.2. Not for admission; simply for reference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at 244.1, this is -- it purports to be candidates for some legal organs for HZ HB, a nomination that is coming from Zenica, presumably, and it is -- it should be signed by Dominik Sakic as president; however, your signature appears there. Could you explain that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not remember this document. This is not a document of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is not your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The signature could be, but the document is not mine, for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at the next document, 451.2, dated 8 February 1993, this bears a joint signature, both for yourself and for Dominik Sakic. Why did you have to add your signature to this? Explain that, please. Actually, if you don't mind taking a minute and just reading, quickly, the paragraphs. They're very short.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the document be placed on the ELMO as well, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document speaks of an initiative of the commands of the brigades of Zenica and Vares, to have a joint meeting held, where the current military and political situation would be considered in the areas of the municipalities of Zepce, Maglaj, Zavidovici, Kakanj, Vares, and Zenica, as well as the possibility of cooperation and links between the mentioned municipalities. It is correct that I designed this, and the president of the HVO too. I think this was after the Vance-Owen Plan, or before the Vance-Owen Plan. It speaks of the municipalities that were supposed to be part of a special separate province. Today it is also a single province.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you would be kind enough, as I asked you, just to read the centre paragraph, "Sosenuca" [phoen], from that point on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "The meeting will be held on Thursday, the 11th of February, 1993, beginning at 12.00 at the Croatian House, the former culture centre, and it should be attended by representatives of the commands of the brigade, presidents of the HVO, and presidents of the HDZ party of the above-mentioned municipalities."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You had made reference to the district military courts, and it was your evidence that those had no influence by any political figures. Can I ask you, please, have you familiarised yourself with the Narodni list, which deals with the decree on district military courts for Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall. I know it was published, but I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall who appoints the judges to the district military courts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know. That was never my own province of work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Then you're hearing for the first time as I tell you that the Presidency of HZ HB appoints judges and lay judges to the district military courts upon the recommendation of the head of the Defence Department for the HZ HB; that is your evidence? This is the first time you've heard that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that district military prosecutors are appointed by the military, and at the top it is quite possible that there is a supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, except we were talking about district military courts, which I believe is what you had referred to, but thank you. A quick question about a gentleman you referred to in your evidence named Dragutin Zvonimir Cicak. When did you arrive back on the territory of Bosnia exactly from your time in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the territory of Bosnia. That is where I served in the former JNA. I was trained in Sabac, and I returned from there on the 4th of December, 1991. That is when I was appointed company commander in the territory of Bihac, which is the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you keep yourself current about developments in Busovaca in 1991? Were you following any of the newspapers or did you follow any of the electronic broadcasts or media broadcasts concerning the political situation in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During 1991, Your Honour, I was undergoing training and I lived in Sarajevo. There was very, very little talk of Busovaca. Busovaca is a tiny town on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you had not followed the discourse in the media between Dario Kordic and Dragutin Cicak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you were not aware of the threats made by Mr. Kordic to Mr. Cicak in writing that were published?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I state with responsibility that I was not familiar with any altercations. I only know about the tour of the army, and there was a delegation there that Cicak was on. And it is only then I realised how much hatred he had for Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then your answer --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Busovaca --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, please finish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Busovaca. I really did not know about any of this. I finished. The reasons for Mr. Cicak's animosity are quite unknown to me, and I'm not aware of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you offended by Mr. Cicak, who is a Bosnian Croat or a Bosnian of Croatian extraction, appearing before you in an army -- or in a TO uniform? Did that offend you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did offend me, as a person and as a Croat. The man who was president of the HDZ, and he told me then that he was president of the HDZ in Busovaca, and then that he transferred to the Territorial Defence and started making false accusations, I could not understand that, and that offended me as a man and as a commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question to you is did it offend you because he was a Croat and that he was in a uniform that was associated with perhaps not the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I did not discuss that at all, nor did I think about it at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it offend you that Stjepan Siber is a Croat who is also high ranking in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What offended me was that Colonel Stjepan Siber was a member of the army at the time when we Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina were subjected to aggression and, one could say, destruction by the army of Bosnian Serbs, first and foremost, and after that also the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, at any time when you left the JNA, ever consider joining the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because at the very outset, Your Honours, it was quite obvious where things were heading in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Territorial Defence was a farce. The army of Bosnia-Herzegovina developed out of the Patriotic League, that is, the military branch of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you were released from captivity, are you aware of any investigations that were done into the circumstances surrounding your kidnapping? Specifically, I would like to ask you to take a look at Z658.1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I am familiar with all of this. I gave these documents to the representative of this Honourable Court, Mr. Stefan Obers, and not only this but also many other documents, on the basis of which criminal proceedings were initiated before the municipal court -- the district court in Travnik, with its temporary seat in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then this document, which is dated 15 April, represents the effort by the officials in Zenica, it appears spanning a number of ethnicities from the names, to look seriously into the circumstances surrounding your kidnapping, is that correct, a real investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shows that this is an on-site investigation report of the investigating judge of the district military court in Zenica. The district military court in Zenica was established by the representatives of the army. At that time, already over 97 per cent of its members were Muslim at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever received any awards for your military role from the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, from the Republic of Croatia I received a medal for participation in the liberation operations, Summer and Storm, and I also have the decoration of the Croatian trefoil.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Exhibit Z1476.2, please. This document appears only in the original language, Your Honours. I believe that the explanation of the witness will give it sufficient English and/or French background so that it will be clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at entry number 82 of this document, that is your name; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May we have it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have already said that I was appointed -- that is, decorated with the order of the Croatian trefoil, and that is under entry 82. That is my name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what does it say under your name and your serial number? Could you read, please, the very brief line under it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "The commander of the military district of Vitez." At that time, I was with that command, and throughout the war I was there, since my exchange, until 1997.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Court, please, what the Croatian order of the trefoil is and for what it is awarded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I really cannot answer that question, because I do not know for what it is awarded. But I believe it is awarded for the promotion of Croat interests, and this came as a result -- that is, the decision on decorations resulted from national liberation operations in north-western Bosnia, where on the basis of the Split agreement it had been agreed that the Croatian army units could enter the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina to help with the liberation of parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, territories until then occupied by the army of Bosnian Serbs. After the conclusion of the Dayton Accords, all these units were withdrawn, were pulled out from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they were only in the territory of north-western Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who signed this document, giving you an award the nature of which you do not know, but whose signature appears on the very last page of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The president of the Republic of Croatia, late Dr. Franjo Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The last exhibit, Z1466.2. It has a summary translation attached to it, Your Honours. I hope that that will suffice for the purposes of the questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, these are concerning the military district of Vitez. Your name appears on the first page in the Croatian language, if I am correct, the one sort of in the middle under "B". You are the fifth person down, is that correct, and that is your signature next to your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not understand that question, but it is true that I am here under number 5, --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- which means nothing. This simply means that we were receiving the rank insignia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And above you, under "Section A", the third name down for receipt of rank insignia on the rank of brigadier is the name of Dario Kordic, bearing a signature next to it. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see that name, I see the signature, but I do not know if that is his signature. And after all, politicians may also be awarded ranks without, however, having a commanding role.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the rank that you were afforded was -- you took it seriously and you carried out the duties of that rank, did you not? This was a serious document, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever at any time had any discussion with Colonel Dario Kordic about his relationship with Mate Boban? You have indicated you have never met Boban. Have you ever talked to Kordic about Boban?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never talked about -- discussed Mate Boban with Mr. Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss any matters concerning the late President Tudjman with Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand correctly, you have no knowledge whatsoever of the relationship Dario Kordic had with Mate Boban or with Franjo Tudjman, no knowledge at all; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, how could I know that? I haven't the slightest.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Brigadier Totic, thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give your evidence. It is concluded and you are released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I believe that our next witness is ready. Our next witness is retired Brigadier Luka Sekerija.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Could I ask the Court just to give us a moment? Mr. Nice will be attending. I know he would like to. If it's possible, just for a minute, to make sure he's aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll be waiting for the witness. Let him come too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Take a seat. Yes, Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Sekerija.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I should like to greet all those present in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Will you please be so kind and give us your full name, to begin with.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: I am Luka Sekerija. I was born on the 29th of August, 1954, in the village of Ploca, the municipality of Uskoplje, also known as Gornji Vakuf. I am a Bosnian Croat by ethnicity and I am a Roman Catholic by religion. I am a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you tell us, very briefly, about your education? I will lead you through these questions. I believe there will be no objections to try to finish with this as soon as possible. So you attended your high school at Uskoplje, then a higher administrative school in Novi Sad in Vojvodina; is that so?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I have to remind you. Would you please pause a little before the end of my question and your answers so that you give time to interpreters for that. And tell us about your family life. You are married and you are a father of four. You live in the village of Trnovaca in the municipalities of Uskoplje, don't you?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You are retired at present, but from time to time you work for the municipal government in Uskoplje as an economic advisor, consultant?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And just one thing more. Before you retired from the HVO, you had the rank of an HVO brigadier; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You are the first witness for the Defence to testify about Uskoplje, so could we get just some basic data about Uskoplje, or rather its former name, Gornji Vakuf, although the Court knows now that there are two municipalities; the Croats have the municipality of Uskoplje and the Bosniaks have the municipality of Gornji Vakuf. Could you give us just a few data about the population census of 1991, just roughly. You were about 10.000 Croats in that area. And what about other peoples?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: It is true that there was over 10.000 Croats, that is 10.700, about 3.000 [as interpreted] Bosnian Muslims, and about 1.000 Serbs and others, a small number of others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In the village in which you were born, the village of Ploca, which people were in the majority there?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: It was a purely Croat village. In that area where I was born, the population was entirely Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And what about the results of the first multiparty elections, which also took place in the municipality of Uskoplje in late 1990?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Well, let me see. The principal party of Bosnian Croats, the Croat Democratic Union, won about 45 per cent of all the Croat voters. The party of Bosnian Muslims, the Party for Democratic Action, won about 50 per cent. On the basis of these results, HDZ and the SDA set up their joint government in Uskoplje. The mayor was a Muslim, Muhamed Palalic, and the president of the municipal government, or the executive order as it was called then, was Zdravko Batinic, and he was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Let us go back to your biography, and I am referring to the chapter entitled "Service in the TO," paragraph 9. Mr. Sekerija, between the 10th of September, 1974, until the end of November, 1975, you attended a school for infantry reserve held by the former JNA in the town of Bileca in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that so?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And when you completed that school, you joined the Territorial Defence in Gornji Vakuf as a professional?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And with the Territorial Defence in Uskoplje, you served for some 15 years; that is, from the 20th of September, 1976 until September 1991?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And at the end of that period of time in your career, what rank did you have then?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: When I left, the Territorial Defence was just a matter that it fell apart. In the former system I had the rank of the captain, first class.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In the Territorial Defence, throughout your service with it, there were other professionals in addition to yourself. You were about 11 professional officers all together in it?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And who were commanders during that time while you served with the TO?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: I had 11 colleagues with me. Nine of them were Bosnian Muslims, one Croat, and myself as a Croat. As a Croat, I could never become the commander of that Territorial Defence staff, or rather the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: They were all Muslims, including the last one, Fahrudin Agic, who kept that duty until the outbreak of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. We can move on to the next chapter, paragraph 12. So you put an end to your career with the Territorial Defence in December 1992, and already in April 1992 you joined those early national organisations of you, the Croats, and went to fight on Kupres, where the army of Bosnian Serbs had already undertaken military operations?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Yes, because the boundary between my territory, my municipality and Kupres, these two municipalities are adjacent, so that, with 70 volunteers, I went to help -- I can call it help -- on Kupres, to help fight against the army of Bosnian Serbs, until the 10th of April, 1992, when we withdrew from that area which was taken by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You think in military terms they were superior?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So if I understood properly, the motive which drove you to go and fight against the army -- or rather against the Yugoslav People's Army, which at that time was converted into the army of Bosnian Serbs, was what, defence?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Only the defence of the territory, because, as I said, we have a long boundary we share with Kupres across the Radusa mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And at that time when you joined -- well, HVO; let us call it that. By that time, who commanded the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: When the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia was formed, the first commander was Brigadier Zarko Tole, who stayed there for a while. And after he was captured by the army of Bosnian Serbs, I don't know his fate after that, but I know he spent some time in Bosnian Serb prisons. Towards the end of April he was succeeded as the commander of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia by Ivan Zorica, nicknamed Zulu, and a little later than that, that is in June that same year, he was replaced by Colonel Tihomir Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And when Colonel Blaskic came and he was appointed the commander of the Operative Zone, you were already working in that -- I do not know whether one could call it a staff, but you were there in the early stages of this toja [phoen], weren't you?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And in this Operative Zone of Central Bosnia staff, you were there sometime between May 1992 until about January 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, where were the headquarters of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone in those early days when you joined it?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: The Operative Zone of Central Bosnia was formed, as I have already said, by Mr. Brigadier Zarko Tole, and his seat was at the Jasa factory in Uskoplje. And I was then appointed to the same duty as the head of that command. And the operations officers, late Zvonko Fontana, artillery man Salih Omerovic, who was killed by the Chetniks on Radusa, and we tried to set up that Operative Zone. Very quickly, in no time at all, after about ten days of our work, the army of Bosnian Serbs captured Zarko Tole and took him to prison. And Zulu was appointed to the post of the commander. He was there for a while. And in late June that same year the commander of the Operative Zone Central Bosnia was taken by the then Colonel Tihomir Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, please, where did the headquarters move when Tihomir Blaskic came to head it?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: About ten days or a fortnight after Colonel Blaskic came to -- had that staff, it moved to Motel Lovac in Kruscica, in the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And after that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: And after that, when they were pushed out of that area, the command moved to the Vitez Hotel in Vitez. I believe it was also called Vitez. And it was there until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You told us a moment ago that you were the head of the staff -- that is, that you worked for the staff and then became the head between May 1952 [as interpreted] and January 1993. But to be accurate, it ought to be said that you were absent from your work for about a month, sometime between September, October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Correct, because I suffered some injuries in Jajce in conflicts with the Bosnian Serb army. My collarbone was broken and I sustained some other injuries in that incident which befell me, and then I had my collarbone, or rather my spine, in cast. And I therefore was on sick leave for a month or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Just to correct one thing. I spoke about May 1992, not 1952, as it says in the transcript. It is obviously a slip. So tell us, please, you were the head of the staff at the time when Mr. Franjo Nakic was appointed to the same office. You met him, you turned over the office to him.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: True, because of the injuries I had sustained, and jobs which required somebody to be there all the time. And at the time I was not really ready because of my personal health problems, so I quit the post of the Chief of Staff in late 1992, or rather early 1993, and I returned to my municipality to Uskoplje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So you introduced Mr. Nakic to the job and you left for a month or so. So tell us, when you went back to your municipality, to Uskoplje, tell us, you became the Chief of Staff in the Dr. Ante Starecevic Brigade, and it was commanded by whom?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: It was commanded by Totic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Just very briefly -- I'm moving on to paragraph 17 -- what was the composition of the Ante Starcevic Brigade? Who were the members of that unit? But will you please remember that you have to wait, before you answer, for the question to be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Very well. All members of the brigade of Dr. Ante Starcevic in Uskoplje were local Croats from the territory of Uskoplje. Amongst those soldiers, there were also several volunteers who had returned from Croatia, from the Croatian army, that had been born in that area. After the war broke out in our country, these self-same returned to the territory of Uskoplje to defend their own homes and families. In Dr. Ante Starcevic's brigade, there were seven such volunteers. Of those seven men, two were killed during the war. One suffered wounding, two left the area and went to third countries, that is, to the United States, and two are still in Uskoplje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Just one more detail related to those men. Were those men privates or were there some officers among them?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: No, there were only privates in the Croatian army. They returned to their municipality, to their home turf, and joined the HVO units in Uskoplje or, rather, to be more specific, the Dr. Ante Starcevic Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And so at the outset when you -- in the early days of the formation of the army, Uskoplje was in the joint Operative Zone of Central Bosnia. But when you became the Chief of Staff of the brigade in late January 1993, the Ante Starcevic Brigade was within a different operative zone; is that so?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Yes, at the time when the Uskoplje Dr. Ante Starcevic Brigade was under the direct command of the Operative Zone of Tomislavgrad and the commander there was then Colonel Zeljko Siljeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Just one question more. And in the military hierarchy, who was the superior command to this Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Well, in the chain of command or, if you like, the command hierarchy, all operative zones were commanded exclusively by the Main Staff of the Croat Defence Council, and it was in Grude at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: To avoid any confusion, the Main Staff of the Croat Defence Council moved from one place to another, it had different seats?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Yes. It was first in Grude, then in Posusje, and then moved to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We can move on. Your Honours, we've reached paragraph 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, please, you lived in that area, you could feel all the predicaments, everything that happened in Central Bosnia. The Court has already heard about what took place -- what happened in Bosnia in '92 and '93, but tell us something about the lot of Croats in that broad area of Central Bosnia, and what did other sides aspire to, especially the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Well, it was like this: In late '92 and early '93, the strategic goal of the Muslim leadership was to expel Croats from the territory of Central Bosnia in order to bring in and settle Muslims in those same lands who had fled from the areas taken by the army of Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, please, about the strategic goals insofar as the military industry is concerned.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Well, they are as follows: The army of Bosnian Muslims, the army of BH, as they called themselves, in order to attain a strategic goal, took all the special-purpose production units -- I mean the armament, the weaponry-producing plants such as the ammunition factory of up to 12.7 in Konjic, and it was Igman Konjic; Bratstvo in Novi Travnik, which made all types of barrels from infantry to cannon to other pieces of weaponry; Slavko Rodic in Bugojno, which made hand-held rocket launchers, 70-millimetre calibre, hand-held defence bomb, M-75, which is prohibited by conventions, all types of fuses and detonating devices for mines, grenades, and so on and so forth. And there was only a small part which was needed to round off this production completely, and that was the factory -- the Vitezit factory of Slobodan Princip Seljo, as it was called in the previous system, in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, please, you were educated, you were a trained officer, and for years you were a trained officer in the army. In your view, had the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina managed to take the Slobodan Princip Seljo factory, what did it mean in military terms?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: It is quite easy to draw a conclusion. They would have the total process of production of military equipment in their own hands, and that would have been sufficient for them to carry out their intention, that is to say, the persecution of Croats in these parts. And I thank God and the people who defended this area for having done so. Had this not happened, God knows where we would have been now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You agree with me that Uskoplje, as a town, was of great strategic importance because it was on one of the main roads linking that part of Bosnia and Herzegovina to a southern part -- that is to say, Central Bosnia, the north, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Many have already said that basically this civil war that was waged, not only in Central Bosnia but elsewhere, was a war for roads.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Well, that's what they called the war, the war for roads, the war for communications that could be taken to pass. That is to say, it was a war for territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes. But as we said, first you have to hold the roads for supplies, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Absolutely, because whoever held the roads had the possibility of procuring all the equipment that was needed by soldiers in war; food, weapons, all other equipment that was needed for waging a defensive war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Sekerija, before we move on to paragraph 21, that is to say, about the conflict that started on the 11th of January, 1993, perhaps a few words about whether there were any meaningful armed incidents before that. Perhaps you have a few examples of this nature.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Yes. The first incident between the Croatian Defence Council and the Muslim army in the area where I was occurred on the 17th of June, 1992, when the Muslim self-styled leader, Hanefija Prijic, nicknamed Paraga, attacked two vehicles in which HVO soldiers were being transported. He disarmed them and put the vehicles into the city swimming pool. There was about 20 or 30 centimetres of water in the pool at the time. I just happened to be there then. I established contact with the Muslim commanders, asking them to do everything to prevent a conflict, and we managed to pacify things and to bring tensions down. We had the first casualties on that day, two Croat soldiers were killed, and we also managed to return the people who were imprisoned. And that is when this distrust and intolerance started between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Also in 1992, there was a major conflict. I personally think that I played a major role in this context, and I convinced the military and political leadership of the Muslims that we should not have a war, because we really did not need a war then or afterwards. We had a common enemy, and they were seven or twelve kilometres away from us, as the crow flies, depending on the terrain. That war would not have brought any good either to Croats or to Muslims. So we managed to agree to reach some kind of agreement, and this was the case until January 1993, when a real conflict broke out and when there were terrible casualties on both sides. I'm going to talk about this conflict later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Of course, we can move on to this part immediately, but perhaps a small detail. The headquarters of your brigade, Dr. Ante Starcevic, was in the same factory, Jasa, where the command of the Operative Zone was before that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, during this conflict that started on the 11th of January, 1993, what was the strength of HVO troops and what was the strength of BH army troops?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Well, this is the way it was: The conflict that started sometime in the evening of the 11th of January, 1993, occurred when the Ante Starcevic Brigade had about 1.000 men. The Muslims had two or three thousand soldiers, and they belonged to the 317th Brigade, and they were commanded by Fahrudin Agic. That is the same gentleman who was my commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, who was your commander in the TO. So please now, in a few words -- this is paragraph 22, Your Honours -- about this attack which occurred on the 11th of January, 1993, who was the attacker and which way did the attack progress?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Well, this is the way it was: I remember this very well. The forces of the army on the territory of Uskoplje attacked all lines and all villages of the Croatian Defence Council. It was an all-out attack from all directions. One should note that the Croatian Defence Council in the territory of Radusa held a front line against the Bosnian Serb army. That's when we had 180 soldiers at that front line. In order to make matters even worse, part of this front line was held by the BH army from Gornji Vakuf. And then they were withdrawn only two days earlier, that is to say in the evening of the 8th of January, 1992, and then there was this empty space. Fearing the worse, that is to say, that the Serbs could take the plateau of Radusa towards Uskoplje, I decided, together with the other leaders around 10.00 or 11.00 in the evening of the night, that there I close the line with 70 or 80 soldiers more. I don't remember exactly, but I needed 70 or 80 soldiers, with equipment, in order to seal off this area where the Muslims were withdrawn. This was done by way of a plan, and -- that is to say, the Muslims attacked this area on the 11th of January, although on that same day Colonel Siljeg, Tokic and I, at the UNPROFOR base and with the assistance of U.N. troops, we negotiated with Selmo Cikotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I do apologise. Let us not go any further. Let us explain a detail to the Judges. You mentioned Radusa. Radusa is a mountain where the front line was between the army of the Bosnian Serbs and you were on the other side?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Your conclusion concerning this -- that is to say, after you were attacked on the 11th of January, you realised, in hindsight, what the reason was why the BH army withdrew from that part of the front line that it held?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, the very fact that three days before the combat operations started, they withdrew their forces from the Radusa plateau and then attacked everything that was Croatian, and this went from Radica Staje [phoen], Humac, Jasminik Skirta [phoen], that was the line that was about seven kilometres long, and this line was held by about 300 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Let's make the transcript as precise as possible. When we talked about Radusa, we talked about a front line between the army of the Bosnian Serbs and you were on the other side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Now let us move on to paragraph 23. As you already said, immediately after you were attacked, you proposed -- let me put it that way -- to have a meeting held, so that you tried to negotiate?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Well, this is the way it was: Your Honours, on that very same day, the commander of the Operative Zone of Tomislavgrad, or of the military district, Colonel Siljeg, Tokic, and I asked the representatives of UNPROFOR to call upon the military part of the Muslim leadership, because I think that tensions were at an all-time high and at any moment there could have been an explosion, and we had to take people to Radusa because this line had been abandoned, we asked the U.N. to organise this kind of a meeting, and they accepted this. They helped us meet at the U.N. base in Uskoplje. The Muslim army was represented by Selmo Cikotic as the main negotiator, the commander of the 317th Brigade, Fahrudin Agic, and also some of his officers. In order to avoid a conflict, we made a proposal to Muslim commanders to form a joint command at this very same moment consisting of Croats and Muslims to work together to reduce the tensions and to tell the people that they should not be afraid, that there should not be a war because that war would not suit either side, to reduce tensions and to have Muslim soldiers return to the front line that they had abandoned. Had there been more goodwill on the part of the Muslim leadership, I think this conflict could have been avoided. The Muslims accepted this officially, but then in the evening on that very same day, they rejected our offer, and they attacked all positions and all villages where there was a majority Croat population.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, please, during these days of war, during this first attack and the fighting that broke out, you had the opportunity of touring some Croatian villages or Croat families, houses in individual villages through UNPROFOR, and you were at the village of Bojska at the beginning of February?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, I omitted to mention that the conflict that broke out on the 11th of January lasted approximately from 40 to 45 days. With the U.N. forces, we heard that all the Croats who lived in the village of Bojska -- that was a majority Muslim village -- were killed. I had the opportunity of going there and seeing things for myself. When we arrived in the village, we saw that all Croat houses had been destroyed, the Catholic cemetery was destroyed, and in the house of 87-year-old Franjo Okadar who lived only with his unmarried daughter, Finka, who was approximately born in 1937 -- I know all of this -- when we entered this house the late Okadar, who had been an immobile person for the past three or four years and who was helped by his daughter who lived with him, I saw a terrible scene. The late Franjo Okadar lay on some kind of a couch or sofa with his throat slit, and all the blood had poured out of it. The corpse was there for about two or three days and all the blood was still there. While his daughter's body was naked from the waist downwards, she laid on the floor dead, massacred. The post-mortem showed that she had been raped. She had over 30 knife stabs on her body. This is one of the terrible scenes that I saw for myself. With your permission, I would like to continue. With the help of the U.N., we wrapped these bodies in blankets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've told us about this. Mr. Naumovski, can we go on to deal with the relevant matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Straightaway, Your Honour. I just have one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In addition to these two Croat bodies which you saw for yourself, there were four other Croats there who had been killed. You heard about them from one of your subordinates; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Yes. When I was up there, a Warrior went there to get the bodies of four other Croats who had lived there, and Pero Midangic [phoen], my subordinate, went there. I sent him there personally because I couldn't go myself, due to other business I had to attend, and he saw the bodies. And also there is the post-mortem that was conducted by a doctor who was assigned to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So out of all the six Croats who lived in the village of Bojska, all of them were killed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: There were certain incidents in the month of June 1993?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber, as briefly as possible, what happened to a convoy organised by Caritas? The two priests, Friar Vinko Tomas and Friar Nikica Milicevic, were taken through Uskoplje towards Fojnica?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your permission, I don't want to move on to the next point until I say the following: When these convoys ended without anyone winning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sekerija, you have to realise we have rules here, and one of them is to stick to what is relevant. If counsel wants to ask you about something, he will, or the Prosecution may cross-examine you. But we'll get on more quickly if you would just answer the questions that you are asked. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Naumovski. What was the point that you wanted? You were going to ask about the convoy?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sekerija, I asked you about this convoy. Could you please tell the Honourable Judges what happened and under what circumstances it came?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: The convoy came from the direction of Vrana, and it was stopped in the village of Bidris [phoen], where the HVO had control. This was an exclusively humanitarian convoy, and it was led by Friar Vinko Tomas and the late Friar Nikica Milicevic, who was killed by Muslims in the church in Fojnica. As I passed through this area, I personally ordered that the convoy should not go through Muslim-held territory, although it had to go that way, until we reached agreement on this, until we asked them to let this convoy pass through, because this was exclusively for humanitarian assistance. In spite of my warning, Friar Vinko Tomas, believing he was a servant of God and that the Muslims would not do anything to him, as they entered the town that was Muslim-held, they took the convoy, they beat up all the drivers, they took all the goods, and then for five or six days we had an exchange for these people. We asked for them to be returned to us, although they had been beaten so badly. So this went on for five or six days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. We can proceed chronologically now. Again there was an attack on the HVO in June 1993, that is to say, on the 24th of June; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Who attacked, and how long did the fighting go on, and did it stop at all until the ceasefire was signed in the spring of 1994?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Before this conflict broke out on the 24th of June, 1993, I was imprisoned by Muslim soldiers as I was touring the Radusa front line in a village -- I don't want to talk about this because nobody asked me about it, but I'm going to say something else. On the 24th of June, 1993, in the afternoon hours, the villages of Kute, Vaganjac, Gaj and Gornji Fojnica were attacked by all weapons that were available, and the commander of the Muslim unit was Hanefija Prijic, nicknamed Paraga. This was the second time that he appeared as a local sheriff, taking justice into his own hands. I don't know whether he was under direct command, but he did have means of communication to communicate with his commander, Agic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Perhaps you could tell us quite briefly, the gentleman that you just mentioned now, let us say a few words about his unit, under quotation marks. There are some incidents that are linked to it that occurred in Pavlovica?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Yes. Uskoplje, Novi Travnik, across Pavlovica, is an area where many people disappeared. This gentleman Hanefija Prijic, nicknamed Paraga, is one of the leaders of these groups. He was a highwayman. There is no other word for him and for them, these people who committed all these atrocities. Italian Caritas was going through this area, and they imprisoned them. And also Mijo Milic was massacred, and the driver, and killed. The Italian member of Caritas just happened to remain alive. When we finally got him, he reached our positions, we didn't understand what he was saying, but we found an interpreter. The Italian told us that all his colleagues had been killed, that the vehicle was taken away as well. There is a video cassette, and we assumed that this was the one and the same group that was doing this all the time, the one led by Hanefija Prijic. When he saw this videotape that we wanted to show him, then he said this was the man who did it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Naumovski, it's very difficult to follow this sort of evidence. Perhaps you could just bring the witness to deal with what is relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. These were just certain incidents that preceded this. But now let us move on to a day of bloodshed, the day of greatest bloodshed for the Croats in Uskoplje. Your Honours, this is paragraph 27, that is to say, the events of the 4th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Could you tell us, briefly, how many civilian casualties there were, what kind of an attack this was, but as brief as possible, please.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Your Honours, on the 4th of August, 1993, Bugojno and Travnik had already fallen to the Muslims, one of the bloodiest and most difficult attacks on this front line started. Twelve civilians were killed on that day, seventeen soldiers were killed, and forty-seven wounded. The forces of the army in Uskoplje, rather, in Gornji Vakuf, that is to say, the locally based 317th Brigade, were reinforced with other Muslim troops, the Mujahedin units, and units of the 17th Krajiska Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: During those days, you were heavily wounded yourself?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Yes. On that very same day, to be more precise, I was driving in a tank, because it was impossible to pass otherwise because of all the gunfire, the gunfire coming from the Muslim side. And at that point the tank, T55, was hit by a Milutka [phoen] anti-armour projectile. The projectile was fired from Muslim sides and it hit the tank, where there were four soldiers and myself. Two soldiers burned down completely; two were heavily wounded, as I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Not to go into all the details -- all of this was mentioned in paragraph 27 -- but as a result of this, you are a disabled person by 80 per cent, due to the injuries that you sustained on that day?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
utterances.text: Yes. Due to the injuries I sustained on that day, I am a permanent invalid, 80 per cent. Your Honours, with your permission, I wish to mention a report of the UN forces. They sent the UN headquarters, through their own chain of command, I imagine, and I personally saw a copy of this document that was written in English but that was translated into the Croatian language as well. And I quote it: "The Uskoplje front line at the moment is the strongest concentration of manpower and technical equipment." And now something else which is very important. "Uskoplje is being attacked by 19.000 to 23.000 Muslim soldiers, and it is being defended by 1.800 to 2.500."

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. We don't have to go into all the details.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SEKERIJA
